parts.title: Booking a room for a family celebration
parts.intro: Part 1. You will hear a man phoning a hotel to book a room for a family celebration.

lines: SARAH: Good afternoon, Riverside Hotel, events team. Sarah speaking.
DANIEL: Hello. I'm calling about hiring a room for a family party. It's for my parents' fortieth wedding anniversary.
SARAH: Congratulations to them! I can certainly help. Can I start with your name?
DANIEL: Yes, it's Daniel Fenwick. That's F-E-N-W-I-C-K.
SARAH: Thank you, Mr Fenwick. And what date were you thinking of?
DANIEL: We'd originally hoped for Saturday the fourteenth of June, but my sister can't come that weekend, so it'll have to be the twenty-first.
SARAH: The twenty-first of June. Let me check. Yes, we have two rooms free that evening. How many guests are you expecting?
DANIEL: We've invited about sixty people, but I think around fifty will actually come.
SARAH: Then I'd suggest the Garden Room. The Lake Room is bigger, but it holds a hundred and twenty, and it would feel rather empty with fifty. The Garden Room is ideal for up to seventy.
DANIEL: That sounds right. Does it have its own entrance? Some of the older relatives use wheelchairs.
SARAH: It has step-free access from the car park, and there's a lift to the main restaurant if you need it.
DANIEL: Perfect. And what's the cost for hiring it?
SARAH: For an evening, the room itself is three hundred and fifty pounds. That's reduced to two hundred and eighty if you book our catering as well.
DANIEL: We'll probably want catering, so that's good news. Do we have to pay a deposit?
SARAH: Yes, we ask for a deposit of one hundred pounds to confirm the booking, and the rest one week before the event.
DANIEL: Can you tell me about the food options?

SARAH: Of course. There are three menus. The buffet is the most popular for family parties. It's twenty-two pounds per person and includes hot and cold dishes. A sit-down dinner is thirty-five pounds, and there's also a lighter afternoon tea menu at fifteen.
DANIEL: I think the buffet would suit us best. My parents would like a cake, though. Can we bring our own?
SARAH: You're welcome to bring a cake. We just ask that you let the kitchen know in advance, and there's no extra charge for serving it.
DANIEL: Great. What about music? My cousin is a DJ.
SARAH: That's fine, but the music has to finish by eleven o'clock, because we have guests staying in the rooms above. The room itself is yours until half past eleven, so there's time to clear up.
DANIEL: That's reasonable. And decorations?
SARAH: You can decorate the room, but please don't use anything that sticks to the walls. We provide white tablecloths, and we can arrange fresh flowers on the tables for an extra forty pounds.
DANIEL: I'll talk to my sister about the flowers. One last thing: is there parking for guests?
SARAH: Yes, guests can park for free in the hotel car park. If it's full, there's a public car park on Bridge Street, about five minutes' walk away.
DANIEL: Lovely. I think that's everything for now. Could you send me the booking form?
SARAH: Of course. I'll email it to you this afternoon.

parts.title: A new community park
parts.intro: Part 2. You will hear a park manager talking to local residents about a new community park.

lines: TONY: Good evening, everyone, and thank you for coming. I'm Tony Hale, the manager of the new Hilltop Community Park, which opens to the public next month. Tonight I'd like to show you around the park on the plan, and then tell you about some of the activities we're planning.

TONY: If you look at the plan, you'll see the main entrance on Park Road, in the bottom left-hand corner. From there, the main path runs straight across the park from west to east, and a second path runs from south to north, crossing it in the middle.
TONY: Just to the right of the main entrance, before you reach the north-south path, you'll find the visitor centre. That's where you can pick up maps and information about events.

TONY: Now, if you follow the north-south path to the very top of the park, you'll come to the community garden. That's on the right of the path, at the far end, and it's where local schools will be growing vegetables.
TONY: Many of you have asked about the children's playground. It's on the left-hand side of the park, just above the main path, so parents can see it easily from the benches there.

TONY: The café is in a lovely position, right next to the lake, on its left side. It's on the far side of the main path from the entrance, so you walk up the north-south path, turn right, and you'll see it in front of the water.
TONY: And finally, the toilets. These are in the north-west corner of the park, at the top on the left, next to the play area for younger children.
TONY: There's one more building I should mention: the small hut beside the lake on its right side. That's the boat hire office, which will open in the summer.

TONY: Now let me tell you about some of the activities we're planning. Several people have asked whether dogs will be allowed. They will, but they must be kept on a lead everywhere except in the open field to the east of the community garden, where they can run freely.

TONY: We'd also like to involve local people as volunteers. We expected that most volunteers would want to help in the garden, and we do need people there, but the area where we're most short of help is actually the visitor centre, especially at weekends, when we need people to welcome visitors and answer questions.
TONY: The park will be open every day from seven in the morning. In summer, the gates will close at nine in the evening, and in winter at five. The café will keep its own hours, opening at nine.

TONY: For the opening day, we've planned a programme of events. There'll be a guided walk around the lake at ten, and a children's treasure hunt at two. We had hoped to have a concert in the evening, but unfortunately the stage won't be ready in time, so that will take place later in the summer instead.

TONY: We'd also like your ideas for the park's name. Hilltop Community Park is only a working title. We'll be collecting suggestions through the council website until the end of the month, and the final choice will be made by a vote of local residents, not by the council.

TONY: And lastly, a request. We're trying to reduce litter, so there won't be bins inside the park, except at the café. We're asking visitors to take their rubbish home with them. We know this is unusual, so we'll see how it works over the first year.
TONY: Right, are there any questions?

parts.title: Preparing a presentation on food labels
parts.intro: Part 3. You will hear two students, Mei and Josh, discussing a presentation they are preparing on food labelling.

lines: MEI: Josh, have you got a minute to go over our presentation? It's only two weeks away now.
JOSH: Sure. I've been reading about traffic-light labels, the ones that show red, amber or green for fat, sugar and salt.
MEI: Me too. What surprised me was that people do look at them, but mostly when they're buying something for the first time. Once they've chosen a product, they hardly ever check the label again.

JOSH: Yes, I read that as well. I'd assumed that the main problem would be that people don't understand the colours, but actually they understand them quite well. It's more that they don't use them regularly.
MEI: So should we focus on that in the presentation?
JOSH: I think so. And we should mention the research on portion sizes. A lot of labels give information per hundred grams, but people eat very different amounts, so the information can be misleading.
MEI: Good point. Now, for our own survey, I was going to interview shoppers outside the supermarket, but the manager said no.
JOSH: That's a pity. What about asking students instead? We could do it in the canteen.
MEI: That's what I was thinking, but students aren't typical shoppers. Maybe we could do an online questionnaire and send it to parents through the school newsletter as well.
JOSH: Good idea. That would give us a wider range of ages.
MEI: Now, how long should the presentation be? The guidelines say fifteen minutes.
JOSH: Fifteen including questions, or fifteen and then questions?
MEI: It's fifteen for the talk itself, then five minutes for questions. So we should aim for about seven minutes each.
JOSH: That's not very long, once we've introduced the topic. We'll have to be selective about the research we include.
MEI: I agree. Let's choose the three most important findings and leave the rest for the questions.
JOSH: Let's decide who does what. I'm happy to do the introduction, since I've read most of the background.
MEI: Fine. And I'll do the part on our survey results, because I'm organising the questionnaire.
JOSH: What about the slides? You're much better at design than I am.
MEI: I don't mind doing them, but you'll need to send me your notes by Friday.
JOSH: No problem. And I think we should both work on the conclusion, so it brings our two parts together.
MEI: Agreed. What about the handout? Dr Lewis said it was optional.
JOSH: I'd rather not have one. People read the handout instead of listening.
MEI: Actually, I think a short one would help, with the main statistics on it. But I'll write it, so you don't have to worry.
JOSH: OK, fair enough. And the practice session? Shall we book a room?
MEI: You know the library staff better than I do. Could you arrange that?
JOSH: Sure. I'll book one of the group study rooms for next Thursday.
MEI: Great. And then we'll rehearse together and time it properly.
JOSH: Sounds like a plan.

parts.title: How honeybees share information
parts.intro: Part 4. You will hear part of a lecture about how honeybees communicate.

lines: LECTURER: Today we're going to look at one of the most remarkable examples of communication in the animal world: the way honeybees tell each other where to find food.

LECTURER: A honeybee colony depends on a group of older workers called foragers. Their job is to find flowers and bring back nectar and pollen. Because flowers in any area bloom and fade quickly, the colony needs a fast way of sharing information about the best places to go.

LECTURER: The solution is a form of movement that scientists call the waggle dance. It was first described in detail in the mid-twentieth century by the Austrian researcher Karl von Frisch, who later received a Nobel Prize for this work.

LECTURER: When a forager returns to the hive with good news, she performs the dance on the vertical surface of the honeycomb, in the dark. She runs forward in a straight line while shaking her body from side to side, then circles back and repeats the movement many times.

LECTURER: The dance contains two key pieces of information. First, the direction of the straight run tells the other bees which way to fly. The bee uses the position of the sun as a reference. If the food is directly towards the sun, she dances straight up the comb. If it's at an angle to the sun, she changes the angle of her run to match.

LECTURER: Second, the length of the waggle run indicates distance. The longer she waggles, the further away the food is. Researchers have estimated that one second of waggling represents roughly one kilometre, although this varies between populations.
LECTURER: Interestingly, the dance also seems to communicate quality. When the food source is particularly rich, the dancer repeats the dance more times, which attracts more followers.

LECTURER: For food that is very close to the hive, usually within fifty metres, bees perform a simpler movement called the round dance, which tells others to search nearby without giving a precise direction.

LECTURER: Not all scientists accepted von Frisch's ideas at first. Some argued that bees found food simply by following smells carried on the dancer's body. The debate was finally settled in the 2000s, when researchers used radar to track individual bees after they had watched a dance. The bees flew directly towards the area indicated by the dance, which would not have been possible using smell alone.

LECTURER: Why does this matter today? Bee populations are under pressure in many parts of the world, and understanding how they find food helps us plan landscapes that support them. Some researchers now decode thousands of dances recorded on video to create maps of where bees are feeding. These maps have shown, for example, that bees in some cities travel surprisingly long distances, which suggests that suitable flowers are scarce.
LECTURER: In our next session, we'll look at how other social insects, such as ants, solve similar problems.

passages.title: Farming upwards: the rise of vertical farms
paragraphs: Inside a converted warehouse on the outskirts of a large city, lettuces are growing on shelves stacked almost to the ceiling. There is no soil, and not a single window admits daylight. Instead, the plants are illuminated by rows of purple-pink diodes, their roots suspended in trays through which a nutrient solution circulates continuously, while sensors record temperature, humidity and carbon dioxide levels every few seconds. Facilities of this kind, generally described as vertical farms, have multiplied rapidly over the past fifteen years, and their supporters claim that they could transform the way in which cities are supplied with fresh food.

The underlying idea is not entirely new. Growing plants without soil, a technique known as hydroponics, has been practised experimentally for well over a century, and commercial greenhouses have used it for decades. What distinguishes the modern vertical farm is the combination of hydroponics with complete control over the growing environment and with artificial lighting efficient enough to replace the sun altogether. The decisive technical development was the falling cost of light-emitting diodes, or LEDs, which convert electricity into light far more efficiently than earlier lamps and emit relatively little heat, so that they can be positioned only a few centimetres above the leaves without scorching them.

Because the environment is sealed, growers are able to adjust conditions to suit each crop precisely. The colour of the light, for example, can be tuned to the wavelengths that plants use most effectively for photosynthesis, which is why most facilities appear pink rather than white. Since pests have few opportunities to enter, pesticides are rarely necessary, and the produce frequently requires no washing before it is eaten. Most strikingly, the water that is not absorbed by the plants is collected, filtered and recirculated, so that a vertical farm may consume as little as five per cent of the water required to grow the same quantity of lettuce in an open field.

Advocates also emphasise the advantages of location. Conventional vegetables are frequently transported hundreds or even thousands of kilometres between farm and supermarket, losing freshness during the journey; a vertical farm, by contrast, can be situated within the city that it supplies, allowing produce to be harvested in the morning and sold the same afternoon. Furthermore, because harvests are unaffected by droughts, floods or unseasonal frosts, output remains consistent throughout the year, an attribute that retailers value highly.

The principal obstacle is energy. Sunlight is free, whereas electric lighting is not, and in most facilities lighting accounts for the largest single share of operating costs, followed by the climate-control systems that remove the heat and moisture generated inside the building. Unless that electricity is derived from renewable sources, the carbon emissions associated with a vertically farmed lettuce can actually exceed those of one grown outdoors and transported a considerable distance. Several well-funded companies have closed in recent years, having discovered that their running costs could not be recovered from the prices that consumers were prepared to pay. Critics also note that the buildings themselves, with their pumps, sensors and specialised equipment, represent a substantial initial investment that must be repaid before any profit is made.

For these reasons, the range of crops that can be grown profitably remains narrow. Leafy greens and herbs are well suited to vertical farming because they mature quickly, occupy little height and consist largely of edible material. Staple crops such as wheat and rice, in contrast, require extended growing periods and produce a high proportion of stalk and straw, which renders indoor cultivation economically unworkable at present. Even tomatoes and strawberries, which a number of companies are now attempting to cultivate, demand substantially more light and space than lettuce does.

Researchers are attempting to address these limitations in a variety of ways. Some are developing plant varieties specifically bred for indoor cultivation, compact enough to fit between closely spaced shelves and capable of growing well under lower light intensity. Others are investigating whether lighting could be concentrated in periods when electricity is cheapest, such as during the night, without reducing yields significantly. A third approach involves locating farms close to sources of waste heat, such as factories or data centres, so that energy which would otherwise be lost can contribute to maintaining suitable growing temperatures.

Whether vertical farms will ever become more than a specialised supplier of salad ingredients remains uncertain. They are unlikely to replace conventional agriculture, which still produces the overwhelming majority of the world's calories. Nevertheless, in cities where land is scarce, the climate is harsh or fresh produce must otherwise be imported over long distances, they may come to occupy a valuable, if limited, place in the food supply, particularly if the cost of renewable electricity continues to decline.

passages.title: The return of the sea otter
paragraphs: Along the Pacific coast of North America, the sea otter has staged one of the more remarkable recoveries in the history of wildlife conservation. Two centuries ago, several hundred thousand of these animals are thought to have inhabited the coastal waters in a broad arc stretching from northern Japan to the Baja California peninsula. Unlike most marine mammals, however, sea otters possess no insulating layer of blubber; instead, they rely on a coat of extraordinarily dense fur, with more hairs per square centimetre than any other mammal, which traps a layer of air against the skin. That same characteristic made their pelts exceptionally valuable to fur traders, and from the eighteenth century onwards they were hunted relentlessly. Historical records from trading companies suggest that tens of thousands of pelts were shipped across the Pacific in some years, a scale of exploitation that few populations of a slow-breeding mammal could withstand.

By the early twentieth century, the species had been reduced to perhaps one or two thousand individuals, scattered among a handful of isolated colonies, and many observers assumed that it was destined for extinction. International protection was finally agreed in 1911, when a treaty between several Pacific nations prohibited commercial hunting. Recovery, nonetheless, proceeded slowly. Sea otters reproduce at a modest rate, typically giving birth to a single pup at a time, and the surviving populations were too widely dispersed to recolonise their former range unaided. In several regions, conservationists eventually relocated animals by boat or aircraft in an effort to re-establish colonies on stretches of coast where the species had disappeared. Some of these translocations failed, as released animals dispersed far from the intended site or failed to survive the stress of capture and transport, but others established colonies that have since expanded steadily along the coast.

As numbers increased, scientists began to observe that the otters' return was transforming entire coastal ecosystems. Sea otters consume large quantities of sea urchins, spiny animals that graze on kelp, the giant seaweed that forms dense underwater forests in cool, shallow waters. Where otters had been eliminated, urchin populations had multiplied unchecked and reduced extensive kelp forests to barren expanses of rock. Where otters were reintroduced, urchin numbers declined and the kelp regenerated, sometimes within a few years. Ecologists cite this sequence as a classic illustration of a 'keystone species', an animal whose influence on its environment is disproportionate to its abundance. The phenomenon has been documented in Alaska, British Columbia and California, and although its details vary from site to site, the general pattern has proved remarkably consistent.

The recovery of the kelp has implications that extend beyond the otters themselves. Kelp forests provide shelter and nourishment for hundreds of other species, including commercially significant fish, and they dampen the force of waves approaching the shore. Kelp also absorbs carbon dioxide as it grows, and some researchers have estimated that the presence of otters may substantially increase the quantity of carbon stored along coastlines where they are found. These calculations remain controversial, however, because much depends on how long the carbon taken up by kelp remains locked away rather than being returned to the atmosphere. Some tourism operators, too, have begun to promote otter-watching excursions, although the economic value of such activities has not been systematically assessed. Even so, the broad ecological benefits of restored kelp forests are now widely accepted among marine biologists.

Not everyone has greeted the otters' return enthusiastically. Shellfish fishermen, in particular, complain that the animals consume the clams, crabs and abalone on which their livelihoods depend, and in some areas the reappearance of otters has coincided with the collapse of local shellfish fisheries. Conservationists respond that these fisheries flourished in the first place largely because the otters had been removed, and that their productivity during the twentieth century was therefore an artificial situation rather than a natural one. Negotiating between these perspectives has become a recurrent source of tension in coastal communities. In parts of Alaska, indigenous communities have also raised the question of whether traditional, small-scale harvesting of otters should be permitted where populations have recovered strongly, a proposal that remains contentious.

Despite its successes, the sea otter remains vulnerable. Because the animals depend on their fur for warmth, contamination by oil prevents it from insulating them, and a single major spill can prove fatal to hundreds of individuals. Disease, frequently associated with pollutants and parasites carried into the sea by rivers and storm drains, has become a growing cause of mortality in certain populations. In some areas, increased predation by orcas, which appear to have turned to otters as their usual prey has declined, has caused sharp and unexpected falls in numbers. The species has therefore been described not as rescued but as recovering, a distinction that conservationists insist upon. Monitoring programmes now track the size and health of the main populations, providing early warning of declines that might otherwise go unnoticed until recovery has been reversed.

passages.title: Should schools still teach handwriting?
paragraphs: In classrooms across much of the world, the pencil is steadily yielding to the keyboard. Children who would once have devoted hours to practising joined-up script now learn to type during their earliest years at school, and a growing proportion of their written work is produced and submitted on screens. Several education systems have already removed cursive writing from the compulsory curriculum, and others are considering whether to follow. Since most adults now write far more on keyboards than by hand, it is tempting to conclude that handwriting has become an obsolete skill, retained largely out of nostalgia. I believe that conclusion is premature, although not for the reasons most commonly advanced by its opponents.

The case for handwriting is frequently presented in sentimental terms: a handwritten letter is said to be more personal, a signature an expression of individual character, and fine penmanship a mark of education and discipline. These arguments may possess a certain charm, but they cannot justify the considerable amount of classroom time that the teaching of handwriting requires. If the only advantages of writing by hand were aesthetic or emotional, schools would be entirely justified in concentrating their limited resources elsewhere. Indeed, by resting the case on such grounds, defenders of handwriting may inadvertently strengthen the position of those who regard it as an outdated accomplishment.

The more persuasive arguments concern learning rather than appearance. A number of studies have found that young children who practise forming letters by hand subsequently recognise them more readily than children who learn the same letters by selecting them on a keyboard. One plausible explanation is that drawing a letter obliges the child to attend to its shape in detail, whereas pressing a key requires only that the correct key be identified. Brain-imaging research has indicated that regions associated with reading become more active after handwriting practice than after typing practice, although such studies have generally involved small numbers of participants and their conclusions should be treated with appropriate caution.

Comparable claims have been made regarding older students. In one widely publicised experiment, university students who took lecture notes by hand performed better on conceptual questions about the lecture than those who typed their notes on laptops. The researchers attributed this to speed: because handwriting is slower, students are compelled to summarise and select rather than transcribe the lecturer's words verbatim, and that process of selection deepens their understanding. Subsequent attempts to replicate the finding, however, have yielded inconsistent results, and it remains possible that the advantage reflects the way in which students choose to use a laptop rather than any inherent property of handwriting itself. It would be unwise, therefore, to treat this single study as decisive evidence that laptops should be banned from lecture theatres, as some enthusiastic commentators have proposed.

There are also practical considerations. In many countries, important examinations continue to be written on paper, and students whose handwriting is slow or illegible may be penalised not for their ideas but for their inability to record them quickly enough. Until such examinations are conducted entirely on computers, abandoning instruction in handwriting would place some students at a measurable disadvantage. It is worth noting, too, that a pen and paper require neither electricity nor an internet connection, a consideration of some significance in schools where access to technology remains unreliable. Teachers also report that students who cannot write fluently by hand often find it more difficult to annotate texts, sketch diagrams or jot down quick notes during discussions, activities that remain a routine part of classroom learning even in schools that are well equipped with computers.

Another consideration, rarely mentioned in public debate, concerns students with particular learning difficulties. For some children with conditions that affect fine motor control, the physical act of writing is so laborious that it obstructs the expression of their ideas, and for these students access to a keyboard can be genuinely liberating. Any sensible policy must therefore allow for flexibility, recognising that the arguments which apply to the majority of learners may not apply to every individual, and that teachers are generally best placed to judge which approach serves a particular child.

None of this suggests that schools should resist the teaching of typing, which is indisputably essential in modern working life. Nor does it require a return to the hours of copying exercises that were once commonplace, many of which were concerned more with uniformity of appearance than with fluency. The objective should be handwriting that is legible and sufficiently rapid to keep pace with thought, not handwriting that is beautiful. Whether that writing is joined or printed is, in my view, considerably less significant than whether the child can produce it comfortably and without conscious effort.

The most sensible approach, then, is not to choose between pen and keyboard but to determine what each does best. Handwriting appears particularly valuable in the early stages of literacy and when the aim is to think and remember, while typing is superior for producing, revising and sharing longer texts. A curriculum that allocates time to both, and that explains to students why each matters, is likely to serve them better than one that treats either skill as a relic or as a substitute for the other. Such a curriculum would also be easier to defend against the charge of nostalgia, since it rests on evidence about learning rather than on attachment to tradition.

task1.prompt: The maps below show the centre of the town of Eastbridge in 2005 and today. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant. Write at least 150 words.

figure.title: Eastbridge town centre
figure.alt: Two maps of Eastbridge town centre. In 2005, a main road crossed the centre from west to east, with a car park in the north-west, a bus station in the north-east, a row of shops along the south side of the road, a market square in the middle of the south, and a factory in the south-east by the river. Today, the main road through the centre is pedestrianised and traffic uses a new ring road to the north; the car park has become a park, the bus station has been replaced by a library, the shops remain, the market square has a new café, and the factory has been converted into apartments with a riverside walk.

task1.model_label: Illustrative model for teacher discussion after the mock. Not a certified band answer.
task1.model:
The maps compare the centre of Eastbridge in 2005 with its layout today.

Overall, the town centre has been transformed from an area designed around traffic into one focused on pedestrians and leisure. Through traffic has been moved away from the centre, and several buildings have been given new uses, although the row of shops has remained unchanged.

In 2005, a main road ran through the middle of the town from west to east. Today, this road has been pedestrianised, and vehicles instead use a new ring road to the north of the centre. The car park that stood in the north-west has been replaced by a park, while the bus station opposite it in the north-east has made way for a library.

To the south of the main street, the shops are still in the same place, and the market square remains, but a café has been added to it. The most striking change is in the south-east, where the old factory beside the river has been converted into apartments, and a riverside walk has been created along the water.
checklist: Task Achievement: Is there a clear overview of the main changes? Are changes and things that stayed the same both reported accurately?
Coherence and Cohesion: Are the changes grouped logically (for example, by area of the town)?
Lexical Resource: Is the vocabulary of change precise (replaced by, converted into, made way for, pedestrianised)?
Grammatical Range and Accuracy: Are past and present perfect passives used accurately?

task2.prompt: In many cities, traffic congestion is becoming worse every year. What are the main causes of this problem, and what measures could be taken to reduce it? Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience. Write at least 250 words.
task2.model_label: Illustrative model for teacher discussion after the mock. Not a certified band answer.
task2.model:
Traffic congestion has become a daily frustration for residents of many growing cities, wasting time and polluting the air. In my view, the problem is caused mainly by rising car ownership and poorly planned urban growth, and it can be reduced through better public transport and policies that make driving into city centres less attractive.

The most obvious cause is the rapid increase in the number of private cars. As incomes rise, more families can afford a vehicle, and many see it as more comfortable and convenient than a crowded bus. A second cause is the way cities have expanded. When new housing is built on the edges of a city, far from offices, schools and shops, residents often have no realistic alternative to driving. Finally, in many places public transport is slow, unreliable or simply unavailable, which pushes even more people into their cars.

Several measures could help to address these causes. The most effective long-term solution is to invest in fast and frequent public transport, such as metro lines and dedicated bus lanes, so that people have a genuine choice. Governments could also discourage unnecessary car journeys by introducing charges for driving into the busiest areas at peak times, as some European cities have done with considerable success. In addition, urban planners should ensure that new neighbourhoods include workplaces, schools and services, reducing the distances people need to travel.

In conclusion, congestion results from a combination of more cars, scattered development and inadequate public transport. Tackling it requires a combination of improved alternatives to driving and measures that make car use in city centres less convenient.
checklist: Task Response: Are both parts of the question (causes and measures) answered fully, with each measure linked to a cause?
Coherence and Cohesion: Is there one main idea per paragraph, with clear progression?
Lexical Resource: Is vocabulary on transport and cities precise (congestion, peak times, public transport, urban planning)?
Grammatical Range and Accuracy: Are complex sentences, modals and conditionals controlled?
